title: Polestar Loses US Market Access Under Connected Vehicle Rule While Geely Sibling Volvo Gets a Pass
summary: The Bureau of Industry and Security denied Polestar authorization to sell electric vehicles in the US from model year 2027 onward over its ownership ties to China's Geely Group — even as Geely sibling Volvo won authorization a month earlier. BIS has not explained the split, raising questions about how consistently the Connected Vehicle Rule's case-by-case process is applied.
body:
Polestar will not be selling new cars in the United States much longer.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) denied Polestar's request for authorization to sell connected vehicles in the US beginning with model year 2027, the company confirmed on June 25. The denial invokes the Connected Vehicle Rule, finalized in January 2025, which restricts the sale of vehicles with “sufficient nexus” to China or Russia — covering software in MY2027 and hardware from 2030.

The trigger is ownership, not assembly. Polestar's Polestar 3 rolls off the same South Carolina line as the Volvo EX90; the Polestar 4 is built in Busan, South Korea. Neither vehicle is made in China. But Polestar is majority-owned by Geely, the Chinese automotive group, and under the Connected Vehicle Rule that link to Chinese corporate control is sufficient to disqualify the brand.

That interpretation becomes harder to defend when you look at what happened to Volvo.

Volvo — also majority-owned by Geely — received BIS authorization in May 2026, about a month before Polestar was denied. Volvo attributed the result to a process carried out case-by-case, describing authorization as the outcome of “constructive discussions with the US Department of Commerce and other US officials regarding Volvo Cars' governance, technology and data security,” according to the company's statement as reported by Yahoo Finance and CNBC. A Volvo spokesperson told The Drive the company had “no insight into Polestar's authorization approval process.” BIS has not publicly explained what distinguished the two cases.

Polestar announced it will sell through remaining US inventory of the Polestar 3 and Polestar 4, and will continue servicing existing owners through its network. The company's press release described the outcome as a strategic pivot, announcing it would strengthen its focus on Europe. The US already represented a thin slice of Polestar's business: 94% of the company's Q1 2026 retail sales came from outside the US, with Europe accounting for close to 80% of retail volumes. The company has announced localized European manufacturing for the upcoming Polestar 7. Polestar shares fell more than 13% following the announcement.

The Geely/Volvo split is the part of this story that resists a clean explanation. The Connected Vehicle Rule's standard is “sufficient nexus” to Chinese entities; both brands share a parent. That one passed the standard and the other did not — with BIS declining to detail the reasoning — raises legitimate questions about whether the authorization process is applied consistently. A Polestar spokesperson declined to speculate on future manufacturing options when asked by The Drive.

The Connected Vehicle Rule was designed to address a genuine concern: connected cars collect sensitive location, movement, and biometric data, and software pipelines to Chinese-controlled servers represent a specific and documented risk. The rule's proponents argue the case-by-case authorization process is the right tool, allowing brands that can demonstrate adequate governance controls to continue operating. Skeptics will read the Polestar outcome as evidence that the process rewards corporate relationships over demonstrated risk mitigation — a concern the opacity of this decision will not put to rest.

Polestar's exit from new US sales is a concrete outcome. The reasoning behind it remains officially unaccounted for.
ai_monologue: The story is clear on what happened; what's missing is why Volvo passed and Polestar didn't — BIS isn't saying, and “constructive discussions” is not a legal standard. The Geely/Volvo split is the most important detail in the brief, and it's also the one with the least official daylight.
ai_monologue_extended: I received a verified brief at 0.95 confidence from the Source Checker, confirmed across 12+ outlets. Draft v1 contained two source-contradicting errors caught by the Article Verifier: I silently compressed the Volvo authorization quote, and I misattributed the 94% retail figure to Europe specifically. Both are corrected: the Volvo quote is now byte-equal to the Yahoo Finance/CNBC source, and the 94%-outside-US / ~80%-Europe distinction is properly attributed to Electrek. My main residual uncertainty is BIS's stated rationale: no source I accessed reproduces the denial letter directly, so “sufficient nexus” is attributed throughout to the rule's text, not to BIS's specific grounds for denial. The Geely/Volvo split is the spine of the piece, and I've been careful to present the consistency question as an attributed concern rather than an asserted conclusion.
